title: Consistency Models
description: Compare strong, eventual, and causal consistency and know when each is appropriate.

data.text: Consistency is often treated as a binary property, but it is really a spectrum of guarantees about what a read can return. Strong consistency guarantees every read sees the most recent write. Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new writes occur, all replicas will converge to the same value. Causal consistency sits between them, ensuring that writes that are causally related are seen in order by all nodes.

rows: Every read returns the latest write; linearizable.
Replicas converge eventually; reads may be stale.
Causally related writes are ordered; unrelated writes may be seen in any order.

data.caption: Consistency models placed on a spectrum from strongest to weakest.

    C -->|weaker| E((Eventual))

data.text: Strong consistency is the easiest for application developers because it behaves like a single shared register. However, it requires coordination across replicas for every read and write, which increases latency and reduces availability during partitions. Eventual consistency is the most available and partition-tolerant, but it forces application logic to handle conflicts and stale data.

data.title: Watch for Stale Reads
data.text: Eventual consistency does not specify when convergence happens. In high-traffic systems, replicas may be stale for seconds or minutes. Always measure your replication lag before relying on eventual consistency for critical user flows.

Causal consistency uses vector clocks or version vectors to track which writes might have influenced others. If user A replies to user B's post, the system guarantees all nodes see B's post before A's reply. However, two users posting unrelated status updates on opposite coasts may see each other's posts in either order. This model is powerful for collaborative applications because it prevents nonsensical ordering without paying the full cost of global synchronization.

terms.definition: A data structure that captures causal relationships between events in a distributed system.
The strongest consistency guarantee: every operation appears to take effect atomically at some point between its start and end.
The delay between a write on the primary and its appearance on a replica.

items.question: Which consistency model should I pick for a chat app?
items.answer: Causal consistency is often ideal. It ensures message order within a conversation without requiring global synchronization across all conversations.

items.question: Can a database offer multiple consistency models?
items.answer: Yes. DynamoDB offers eventual, strong, and bounded staleness consistency. Choose per-operation based on your tolerance for latency and stale data.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Consistency is a spectrum: strong, causal, eventual, and more.
Strong consistency sacrifices latency and availability.
Eventual consistency maximizes availability but requires conflict handling.
Causal consistency balances ordering guarantees with performance.
data.takeaway: Pick the weakest consistency model that still meets your correctness requirements.
